L17@P0: Abstract. Inference-time alignment for diffusion models aims to adapt a pre-trained diffusion model
L18@P0: toward a target distribution without retraining the base score network, thereby preserving the generative
L19@P0: capacity of the base model while enforcing desired properties at the inference time. A central mechanism
L20@P0: for achieving such alignment is guidance, which modifies the sampling dynamics through an additional
L21@P0: drift term. In this work, we introduce Doob’s matching, a novel framework for guidance estimation
L22@P0: grounded in Doob’s h-transform. Our approach formulates guidance as the gradient of logarithm of an
L23@P0: underlying Doob’s h-function and employs gradient-penalized regression to simultaneously estimate
L24@P0: both the h-function and its gradient, resulting in a consistent estimator of the guidance. Theoretically,
L25@P0: we establish non-asymptotic convergence rates for the estimated guidance. Moreover, we analyze the
L26@P0: resulting controllable diffusion processes and prove non-asymptotic convergence guarantees for the
L27@P0: generated distributions in the 2-Wasserstein distance.
L28@P0: Keywords: Controllable generative learning, inference-time alignment, Doob’s h-transform, convergence rate
L29@P0: 1 Introduction
L30@P0: Diffusion models (Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015; Ho et al., 2020; Song and Ermon, 2019; Song
L31@P0: et al., 2021) have emerged as powerful generative tools for sampling from data distributions,
L32@P0: achieving remarkable success across diverse domains, including text-to-image and text-tovideo generation (Ramesh et al., 2021), Bayesian inverse problems (Chung et al., 2023; Song
L33@P0: et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2025; Chang et al., 2025b), and scientific applications (Bao et al.,
L34@P0: 2024; Li et al., 2025; Si and Chen, 2025; Ding et al., 2024b; Uehara et al., 2025a). Recent years
L35@P0: have witnessed the development of large-scale diffusion models pre-trained on vast datasets.
L36@P0: Despite the robust capabilities of these base models in capturing the training distribution,
L37@P0: the target distributions of downstream generative tasks rarely align perfectly with this base
L38@P0: distribution. For example, in conditional generative learning (Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021; Ho
L39@P0: 1
L40@P0-1: arXiv:2601.06514v1 [stat.ML] 10 Jan 2026Chang, Duan, Jiao, Xu, and Yang
L41@P1: and Salimans, 2021), base diffusion models generate samples from a mixture of distributions,
L42@P1: whereas downstream tasks require sampling from specific constituent distributions. Similarly,
L43@P1: in posterior sampling contexts (Chung et al., 2023; Song et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2025;
L44@P1: Chang et al., 2025b; Purohit et al., 2025; Martin et al., 2025), the base distribution serves as
L45@P1: the prior, while the target is the posterior defined by tilting the prior with a measurement
L46@P1: likelihood. Furthermore, downstream tasks frequently impose additional constraints, such as
L47@P1: human preferences or safety considerations (Domingo-Enrich et al., 2024, 2025; Uehara et al.,
L48@P1: 2025b; Kim et al., 2025; Sabour et al., 2025; Denker et al., 2025; Ren et al., 2025), which
L49@P1: must be satisfied without compromising the model’s generative quality.
L50@P1: To bridge the gap between base and target distributions, researchers have proposed
L51@P1: numerous alignment methods (Xu et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2023b; Fan et al., 2023; Clark
L52@P1: et al., 2024; Domingo-Enrich et al., 2024, 2025; Uehara et al., 2024b, 2025b). These strategies
L53@P1: generally fall into two categories: fine-tuning and inference-time alignment. Fine-tuning
L54@P1: approaches involve retraining the base score network via supervised learning (Lee et al.,
L55@P1: 2023b), reinforcement learning (Fan et al., 2023; Black et al., 2024; Clark et al., 2024;
L56@P1: Uehara et al., 2024c), or classifier-free fine-tuning (Ho and Salimans, 2021; Zhang et al.,
L57@P1: 2023; Yuan et al., 2023). Despite its conceptual simplicity, fine-tuning presents significant
L58@P1: limitations. First, it often requires a substantial collection of high-quality samples from the
L59@P1: target distribution, which may be unavailable in practical scenarios like posterior sampling.
L60@P1: Second, the computational cost of retraining score networks can be prohibitive, particularly
L61@P1: for large-scale models with billions of parameters (Uehara et al., 2025b). Third, fine-tuning
L62@P1: is vulnerable to over-optimization (Gao et al., 2023; Rafailov et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2025),
L63@P1: where the network overfits to limited target samples or preferences, causing it to “forget”
L64@P1: the valuable prior information encoded in the base model. This degradation undermines the
L65@P1: fundamental advantage of leveraging pre-trained models.
L66@P1: In contrast, inference-time alignment (Uehara et al., 2025b; Kim et al., 2025; Sabour et al.,
L67@P1: 2025; Denker et al., 2025; Ren et al., 2025; Pachebat et al., 2025) eliminates the need to retrain
L68@P1: the base diffusion model. These methods offer substantial computational advantages and
L69@P1: preserve the generative capacity of the underlying model. The core technique is guidance (Jiao
L70@P1: et al., 2025), which incorporates target information by introducing an additional drift term to
L71@P1: the base diffusion model. Within the framework of Doob’s h-transform (Rogers and Williams,
L72@P1: 2000; Särkkä and Solin, 2019; Chewi, 2025), the score function for the target tilted distribution
L73@P1: decomposes into the sum of the base score and a guidance term, where the guidance is defined
L74@P1: as the gradient of the log-Doob’s h-function (Heng et al., 2024; Tang and Xu, 2024; Denker
L75@P1: et al., 2024, 2025). This relationship has also been investigated through the lens of classifier
L76@P1: guidance (Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021), stochastic optimal control (Han et al., 2024; Tang and
L77@P1: Zhou, 2025), and Bayes’ rule (Chung et al., 2023; Song et al., 2023). The primary challenge
L78@P1: lies in accurately estimating this guidance.
L79@P1: Guidance estimation methods can be categorized into two main approaches: approximation and learning. The approximation approach, exemplified by diffusion posterior
L80@P1: sampling (Chung et al., 2023) and loss-guided diffusion (Song et al., 2023), relies on heuristic
L81@P1: approximations that often lead to inconsistencies with the underlying mathematical formulation. The learning approach (Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021; Tang and Xu, 2024; Denker et al.,
L82@P1: 2024, 2025) attempts to learn the necessary components by deep neural networks. Classifier
L83@P1: guidance (Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021) learns Doob’s h-function via a classifier, but this is
L84@P1: effective primarily for discrete labels. Furthermore, the convergence of the plug-in gradient
L85@P1: estimator of the classifier is not guaranteed, potentially undermining guidance reliability (Mou,
L86@P1-2: 2Inference-Time Alignment for Diffusion Models via Doob’s Matching
L87@P2: 2025, Section 3.2.2). To mitigate this, Tang and Xu (2024) estimate Doob’s h-function and
L88@P2: its gradient using separate neural networks, increasing training complexity. While Denker
L89@P2: et al. (2024) directly learn the guidance, their method requires samples from the target tilted
L90@P2: distribution. Denker et al. (2025) attempt to address this data requirement via iterative
L91@P2: retraining.
L92@P2: To address these limitations, we introduce Doob’s h-matching, a novel framework for
L93@P2: provable guidance estimation in inference-time alignment. We propose a gradient-penalized
L94@P2: regression method that simultaneously estimates Doob’s h-function and its gradient, yielding
L95@P2: a consistent estimator of the guidance. When combined with the pre-trained base score,
L96@P2: our method enables efficient sampling from the target distribution without the need for
L97@P2: computationally expensive fine-tuning or access to target distribution samples.
L98@P2: 1.1 Contributions. Our main contributions are summarized as follows:
L99@P2: (i) We introduce Doob’s matching, a novel guidance estimation framework for controllable
L100@P2: diffusion models grounded in Doob’s h-transform. The Doob h-function is estimated via
L101@P2: a least-squares regression approach augmented with a gradient penalty, and the gradient
L102@P2: of the logarithm of the resulting h-function estimator yields an estimator for the Doob’s
L103@P2: guidance. Additionally, this method is derivative-free, meaning it does not require
L104@P2: access to the gradient of the weight function between the target tilted distribution and
L105@P2: the base distribution.
L106@P2: (ii) We establish non-asymptotic convergence rates for Doob’s matching, showing that
L107@P2: the proposed method guarantees convergence of both the h-function estimator and its
L108@P2: gradient. These results provide rigorous theoretical guarantees for Doob’s guidance
L109@P2: estimation (Theorem 4.3). Moreover, we derive non-asymptotic convergence rates for
L110@P2: the induced controllable diffusion models, thereby establishing rigorous guarantees for
L111@P2: the generated distributions in the 2-Wasserstein distance (Theorem 4.5).
L112@P2: 1.2 Organization. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we
L113@P2: provide a brief introduction to diffusion models. In Section 3, we propose the stochastic
L114@P2: dynamics of controllable diffusion models within the framework of Doob’s h-transform, and we
L115@P2: present a practical algorithm to simultaneously estimate Doob’s h-function and its gradient.
L116@P2: Section 4 establishes non-asymptotic error bounds for both the estimation of the h-function
L117@P2: and the induced controllable diffusion models. Finally, concluding remarks are provided in
L118@P2: Section 5. Detailed proofs of theoretical results are deferred to the appendix.

L311@P5: Example 3 (Transfer learning for diffusion models). Diffusion models have achieved remarkable
L312@P5: success in image generation. However, their performance critically depends on the availability
L313@P5: of large-scale training data. In the scenarios of few-shot generation, training diffusion models
L314@P5: solely on limited samples typically results in poor generative performance. To retain strong
L315@P5: generative capability under data scarcity, a common strategy is to transfer expressive diffusion
L316@P5: models pre-trained on large datasets to the target domain (Ouyang et al., 2024; Wang et al.,
L317@P5: 2024; Zhong et al., 2025; Bahram et al., 2026). Formally, transfer learning aims to adapt a
L318@P5: model pre-trained on a large-scale source distribution to a target distribution of much smaller
L319@P5: size and diversity of samples. However, directly fine-tuning a large pre-trained diffusion
L320@P5: model using only limited target samples often leads to severe overfitting (Wang et al., 2024).
L321@P5: To address this issue, transfer learning approaches for diffusion models typically train a
L322@P5: lightweight guidance network on the limited target data and combine it with the pre-trained
L323@P5: base score network, yielding a modified diffusion model capable of sampling from the target
L324@P5: distribution (Ouyang et al., 2024; Zhong et al., 2025; Bahram et al., 2026). Concretely, Ouyang

L334@P6: 3.2 Controllable diffusion models with Doob’s h-transform. In this subsection, we
